CEST-detectable metabolite candidates: liver

3 of 6 candidates clear the simulated with-vs-without contrast threshold (0.5%) at some field strength, by chemical exchange (downfield, +ppm) or by the relayed NOE (upfield, −ppm). 0 fall below it; 3 are unknown because no group had a verified reference rate, so nothing could be simulated. The threshold applies to our own simulation, never to a literature MTRasym.

  • Glycogen: ✓ detectable (both)
  • Mobile protein/peptide amide pool: ✓ detectable (both)

Excluded before simulation (not stored in the tissue): [model's own exclusion] Phosphomonoesters (PME) / phosphodiesters (PDE) / total choline: 31P/1H MRS peak groupings, no definable repeating unit (seen PMID 11859290); [model's own exclusion] Lipid CH2 / total lipid: spectroscopic peak grouping, not a single molecule/polymer; [model's own exclusion] Fructose-1-phosphate: appears only after exogenous fructose loading (PMIDs 5500310, 2506389, 3114246), not a resting parenchymal pool; [model's own exclusion] Urea: liver secretory product released to blood/bile, not stored in parenchyma; [model's own exclusion] Bicarbonate / bile constituents / plasma / CSF: secreted fluids, not stored in liver parenchyma; [model's own exclusion] Phosphocreatine/creatine: negligible in liver (little creatine kinase/PCr); [model's own exclusion] Glutathione (GSH): likely strong >1 mM liver pool but no clean direct mM tissue figure in retrieved abstracts (PMIDs 12171175, 12587718), so not quantified to avoid inventing a number; [model's own exclusion] Glycosaminoglycans (gagCEST): cartilage/disc matrix component, not a physiologically significant liver parenchymal pool - absent for liver

Recommended field strength(s): 0.5 T, 1.5 T, 3 T, 5 T, 7 T

Robustness to input uncertainty: robust

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (alcoholic hydroxyl OH (x3 per glucosyl unit) [hydroxyl]: concentration 245-490 mM, kex fixed at 31850 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown); aliphatic/ring C-H (glycoNOE) [rnoe]: concentration 245-490 mM, kex fixed at 5 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown)) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 1.06-2.07%, 1.5 T: 2.29-4.44%, 3 T: 3.80-7.28%, 5 T: 5.52-10.46%, 7 T: 6.20-11.69%. Threshold 0.5%. Detectable even at the low corner.

Frequency-collision analysis:

  • The rNOE (-1.1 ppm) overlaps the semisolid MT pool (-2.4 ppm) at every field: separation grows only from 83 Hz (1.5T) to 387 Hz (7T) while the combined linewidth stays ~16 kHz, so the two pools never resolve. This is expected for rNOE and is handled by MTRasym integration, not peak resolution.
  • The OH (+1 ppm) blurs with everything at 0.5T (linewidth ~5 kHz) but is negligible at higher field. The OH and rNOE sit on opposite sides of water and do not collide with each other.

Direct water saturation: Swept B1 is 0.25 µT at all fields (10.6 Hz direct-sat bandwidth). The rNOE at -1.1 ppm is 23-258 Hz from water (0.5-7T), well beyond the bandwidth, so no direct-saturation masking. At 0.5T the 23 Hz offset is closest to the 10.6 Hz band, the tightest margin.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat:

  • MAJOR CAVEAT: the rNOE effective transfer rate of 5 s-1 is a class-level value from a generic protein solution phantom (PMID 25996515), NOT measured for glycogen, NOT in liver, NOT in vivo. Glycogen's rNOE efficiency depends on its very high C-H density and high molecular weight, which differ from the generic protein phantom; the in vivo rate could differ substantially.
  • The OH kex (31850 s-1) is Swift-Connick-derived from a mouse glycogen solution phantom (PMID 38933551), pH and field unstated, not a direct CEST measurement. Both borrowed values lower confidence in the absolute simulated contrast, though the in vivo literature confirms GlycoCEST is real and detectable.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 0.5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=500 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — rNOE is a slow effective exchange (5 s-1); minimum grid B1 is optimal because raising B1 adds direct water saturation without improving the relayed NOE (B1-independent in the weak-transfer limit). Tsat is short at 0.5T because the -1.1 ppm offset is only ~23 Hz, close to the 10.6 Hz direct-sat bandwidth; longer saturation erodes contrast.
    recommended sequence: 1.225% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 1.5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=2000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Offset now 69 Hz, well clear of the 10.6 Hz direct-sat band. Minimum B1 still optimal for the slow rNOE relay. 2 s allows near-steady-state NOE buildup (rNOE builds slowly).
    recommended sequence: 2.645% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 3 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Offset 125 Hz, well clear. Minimum B1 optimal for rNOE. 3 s reaches full NOE steady state. Consistent with the ~1 µT TSE CEST protocol in PMID 26334509. The 4.39% contrast is in the right order relative to the ~0.34% GlycoCEST MTRasym in that paper (which includes MT background).
    recommended sequence: 4.388% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Offset 199 Hz. Same rNOE physics; higher B0 gives larger Hz separation so less direct-sat contamination, raising contrast to 6.36%. Minimum B1 retained.
    recommended sequence: 6.363% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 7 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Offset 258 Hz, best Hz separation, maximum contrast 7.14%. Minimum B1 still optimal for the slow rNOE relay.
    recommended sequence: 7.140% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note: The liver literature extracts GlycoCEST via MTRasym integrated over 0.5-1.5 ppm (PMID 26334509, 26391991), appropriate because the rNOE is a broad slow dip, not a sharp peak, and MTRasym subtracts the symmetric MT background. At 0.25 µT direct saturation is minimal so MTRasym approximates the true rNOE contrast. Multi-pool Lorentzian fitting (PMID 39529314, 42076810) is emerging in muscle glycogen and could be adapted, but the validated liver method is MTRasym integration.

Potential clinical impact

glycogen (glycoCEST, 0.5-1.5 ppm): 1 CEST/NOE application and 1 metabolite-change studies verified (0 human, 2 animal; 0 humans, 8 animals; 5 dropped by verification). Strong CEST evidence: glycoCEST applied in human 3T/7T and rat, showing fasting/CCl4 signal loss and post-prandial rise. Solid metabolite-change evidence (13C/1H-MRS, histology) supports altered hepatic glycogen in T1DM glycogenic hepatopathy, NASH (loss) and OSA (accumulation).

Caveats / critique (4 points, 218 words) — 285 mM anhydrous glucose units is at the high end, consistent with fed/post-meal liver; fasting liver can drop to ~50-100 mM. The upper concentration bound of 4…
  • 285 mM anhydrous glucose units is at the high end, consistent with fed/post-meal liver; fasting liver can drop to ~50-100 mM. The upper concentration bound of 490 mM likely overestimates even well-fed tissue. The concentration is exactly what was simulated, so a post-meal value inflates fasting-state contrast. Both group classes are correct.
  • The rNOE C-H pool (glycoCEST) is correctly identified as the dominant hepatic CEST signal, not the fast-exchanging OH. The OH (kex 31850 s-1) is in the fast-exchange/Swift-Connick regime where the 'CEST' contribution is really water-T2 shortening rather than a discrete peak. No exchangeable protons neglected; the C4 glycosidic C-H is non-exchangeable as stated.
  • Liver literature (PMID 26334509, 26391991) quantifies GlycoCEST by MTRasym integrated over 0.5-1.5 ppm (downfield saturation side), consistent with an upfield NOE pool near -1 ppm. The simulated -1.1 ppm rNOE shift is within this window. No in-vivo shift discrepancy found. None. The three alcoholic OH per glucosyl unit and the 7 ring/aliphatic C-H (rNOE) are both captured.
  • Carboxyl/ester protons are absent in glycogen. no SAR or hardware ceiling is applied: the recommended B1/Tsat is the sweep optimum, and deliverability must be checked against the scanner's SAR monitor Reported in glucosyl-unit mM. 3 exchangeable hydroxyl protons per internal glucosyl unit. Human CEST (glycoCEST) validated; direct mM number is rat/ex-vivo.

Mobile protein/peptide amide pool — CEST: ✓ detectable (both)

Concentration: 50.00 mM typical (40-80 mM (mobile backbone amide units, estimate))

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: This is an ESTIMATE, not a measured value. None of the retrieved liver CEST abstracts give a direct mM figure for the mobile amide pool. APTw-CEST at 3.5 ppm is a validated liver signal, but a direct tissue mM is not reported in the searched sources. Liver is protein-dense and a typical mammalian mobile-fraction backbone amide concentration is on the order of tens of mM, so ~50 mM (range 40-80) is an order-of-magnitude estimate the physicist agent should treat with caution.

Recommended field strength(s): 1.5 T, 3 T, 5 T, 7 T

Robustness to input uncertainty: robust

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (aliphatic side-chain C-H (mobile protein rNOE) [rnoe]: concentration 40-80 mM, kex fixed at 5 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown); backbone amide NH (1 per peptide unit) [amide]: concentration 40-80 mM, kex 15-158 s−1) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.31-0.62%, 1.5 T: 0.66-1.31%, 3 T: 0.27-2.81%, 5 T: 0.38-3.92%, 7 T: 0.42-4.35%. Threshold 0.5%. Detectable even at the low corner.

Frequency-collision analysis:

  • CRITICAL: the 3.5 ppm amide has 0.0 Hz separation from the Glutamine amide pool at EVERY field (3-7T), so the two are completely indistinguishable by CEST; any 3.5 ppm APTw in liver reports the combined protein+glutamine amide signal.
  • The rNOE (-3.5 ppm) overlaps the semisolid MT pool (-2.4 ppm): separation 23-70 Hz (0.5-1.5T) vs ~16 kHz linewidth, unresolved at low field, improving to 527-745 Hz at 5-7T but still below linewidth. The amide sits on the negligible far tail of the very broad glycogen OH (+1 ppm).

Direct water saturation: Swept B1 = 0.25 µT (0.5-1.5T, 10.6 Hz band) and 0.75 µT (3-7T, 31.9 Hz band). The 3.5 ppm amide is 73 Hz (0.5T) to 980 Hz (7T) from water, always beyond the direct-saturation bandwidth, so no masking of the exchange contrast.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: The amide kex (65.5 s-1) is a class-level value borrowed from human brain in vivo (PMID 40228056) and an unspecified in vivo study (PMID 23008121), NOT measured for liver protein. Liver and brain pH are both ~7.4 so kex is likely comparable, but the wide kex spread (15-158 s-1) yields a 3T contrast range of 0.27-2.81%. The rNOE 5 s-1 is the generic protein phantom value (PMID 25996515), not liver-specific, not in vivo.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 0.5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=2000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.389% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 1.5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Intermediate exchange (kex ~66 s-1). At 1.5T the 3.5 ppm offset is 221 Hz. The sweep finds minimum B1 (0.25 µT) optimal: for this kex, higher B1 widens the water direct-saturation profile toward the amide without proportional amide-saturation gain. 3 s reaches steady state. Contrast 0.82%.
    recommended sequence: 0.824% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 3 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — 3.5 ppm = 430 Hz at 3T. B1 rises to 0.75 µT because the larger Hz offset tolerates more direct saturation and higher B1 improves amide-pool saturation for intermediate exchange. Matches the ~1 µT TSE APT protocol (PMID 26334509). 3 s steady state. Contrast 1.18%.
    recommended sequence: 1.175% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 5 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — 3.5 ppm = 717 Hz. Same B1 logic; the APT peak shifts up with B0 for intermediate exchange. 3 s steady state. Contrast 1.65%.
    recommended sequence: 1.650% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 7 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — 3.5 ppm = 980 Hz, maximum water separation. B1 = 0.75 µT still optimal; higher B1 would add direct saturation without proportional benefit at kex ~66 s-1. 3 s. Contrast 1.84%.
    recommended sequence: 1.835% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note:

  • MTRasym at 3.5 ppm is the standard liver APT extraction (PMID 26334509, 26391991, 32785767), appropriate for a relatively sharp intermediate-exchange peak well separated from water at clinical B1.
  • However, because glutamine amide shares the exact 3.5 ppm offset, MTRasym (and any extraction method) cannot attribute the signal to protein alone; multi-pool Lorentzian, AREX, or omega-plot all fail to separate two pools at 0 Hz separation. The 0.75 µT B1 at 3-7T matches the ~1 µT TSE protocols in the liver APT literature.

Potential clinical impact

amide (APT, 3.5 ppm): 1 CEST/NOE application and 0 metabolite-change studies verified (0 human, 1 animal; 0 humans, 0 animals; 3 dropped by verification). Strong liver CEST evidence: APTw used to grade human HCC (3T, AUC 0.814, correlated with grade), predict TACE response (combined model AUC 0.851), and detect/track rodent HCC therapeutic response, plus 3T liver reproducibility. Direct free-amide-pool metabolite-change evidence in liver not established (pool inferred from protein).

Caveats / critique (8 points, 399 words) — 50 mM as the CEST-visible mobile amide concentration likely overestimates the truly mobile fraction. Liver protein content is high, but only the mobile (non-sem…
  • 50 mM as the CEST-visible mobile amide concentration likely overestimates the truly mobile fraction. Liver protein content is high, but only the mobile (non-semisolid) subset contributes to the sharp 3.5 ppm APT peak; much of the protein is in the semisolid MT pool. The effective CEST-visible concentration may be 5-15 mM.
  • Since this 50 mM is exactly what was simulated, the 3T contrast of 1.18% may be inflated relative to the mobile fraction. Backbone amide class 'amide' is correct; this is the canonical APT pool. The rNOE class is also correct. No exchangeable protons neglected (one backbone NH per peptide unit plus the rNOE C-H).
  • The amide is the diagnostic group, as argued. The main concern is that 'mobile protein/peptide pool' is not a single chemical entity but a mixture, and the sharpness of the 3.5 ppm line depends on the mobile fraction. Liver APT literature (PMID 26334509, 26391991, 32785767, 36161668) consistently uses 3.5 ppm, matching the simulated shift. No in-vivo discrepancy.
  • Note the simulated kex (65.5 s-1) is a brain-derived class value; liver protein APT kex may differ. None for the backbone amide. Side-chain amide groups (Asn/Gln in proteins) also resonate near 3.5 ppm and are lumped into the APT pool; this is standard and not an error.

  • PubMed's actual title is 'Free-breathing 3D CEST MRI of human liver at 3.0\xa0T.'. extraction_method_citations: PMID 32785767 (claimed as 'APT CEST liver imaging in 203 patients at 3 T (single-slice TSE, breath-hold).') dropped PubMed's actual title is 'Liver MRI with amide proton transfer imaging: feasibility and accuracy for the characterization of focal liver lesions.'.
  • no SAR or hardware ceiling is applied: the recommended B1/Tsat is the sweep optimum, and deliverability must be checked against the scanner's SAR monitor 1 exchangeable amide NH per backbone unit. Human-validated CEST target but concentration is an order-of-magnitude estimate.
  • [Unsourced reasoning] 2 numeric step(s) rest on an unsourced assumption: 'A typical mammalian cell mobile-fraction protein backbone amide pool i'; '1 exchangeable amide NH per peptide-bond (backbone) unit.'.

Recommended field strength(s): 7 T

Robustness to input uncertainty: fragile

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (side-chain primary amide CONH2 (2H) [amide]: concentration 7-20 mM, kex 15-158 s−1) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.02-0.25%, 1.5 T: 0.07-0.73%, 3 T: 0.09-1.40%, 5 T: 0.13-1.95%, 7 T: 0.14-2.16%. Threshold 0.5%. Only the point estimate clears the threshold; the low corner does not.

Frequency-collision analysis: CRITICAL: the glutamine amide at +3.5 ppm has 0.0 Hz separation from the Mobile protein/peptide amide pool at EVERY field (3-7T), so the two pools are completely indistinguishable and cannot be separated by any CEST extraction method. The glutamine is also on the negligible far tail of the very broad glycogen OH (+1 ppm, linewidth ~5111 Hz). The amine group is unsimulated so its collision is unknown. The glutamine amide is effectively unmeasurable independently of protein APT in liver.

Direct water saturation: Swept B1 = 0.5 µT (0.5-1.5T, 21.3 Hz band) and 0.75 µT (3-7T, 31.9 Hz band). The 3.5 ppm amide is 73 Hz (0.5T) to 980 Hz (7T), always beyond the direct-saturation bandwidth, so no masking. The binding constraint is the protein-APT overlap, not direct saturation.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: The amide kex (65.5 s-1) is a brain-derived class value (PMID 40228056, 23008121), NOT measured for glutamine, NOT in liver. Primary amide exchange in glutamine is likely slower than backbone amide, so the borrowed value likely overestimates kex and thus overestimates contrast. The wide kex spread (15-158 s-1) gives a 7T contrast range of 0.14-2.16%. The amine group is unsimulated (no reference), so its exchange rate is unknown and no contrast can be claimed for it.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 3 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.325% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 5 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.455% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 7 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Only 7T reaches the 0.5% threshold (0.505%). At 7T the 3.5 ppm offset is 980 Hz, well clear of water. The amide (if kex ~66 s-1) is intermediate exchange; B1 = 0.75 µT is the sweep optimum and 3 s gives steady state. In practice this signal is completely confounded by the 0 Hz protein-APT overlap and is not a recommended standalone target.

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note:

  • MTRasym at 3.5 ppm would be the natural extraction, but the 0 Hz overlap with protein APT makes it report the combined protein+glutamine amide; no method (MTRasym, multi-pool Lorentzian, AREX, omega-plot) can attribute the 3.5 ppm signal to glutamine alone. Multi-pool Lorentzian cannot fit two components at the same frequency. Glutamine CEST is therefore not an independently quantifiable liver target.
  • The glutamine-amine CEST literature (PMID 27717216, 29626359) targets the amine at ~2-3 ppm in brain phantoms, a different offset from the amide.

Caveats / critique (10 points, 435 words) — 7 mM is within the reported liver glutamine range (~2-10 mM), so the concentration is defensible. At 7 mM the absolute CEST is inherently small: only 7T reaches…
  • 7 mM is within the reported liver glutamine range (~2-10 mM), so the concentration is defensible. At 7 mM the absolute CEST is inherently small: only 7T reaches the 0.5% detection threshold (0.505%). The simulated contrast is exactly proportional to this 7 mM, so a lower true concentration would push the signal below detectability.
  • Primary amide class 'amide' is correct for the side-chain -CONH2. The alpha-amine is correctly classed 'amine' and correctly identified as fast-exchanging/broadened.
  • HOWEVER, the simulated kex (65.5 s-1) is a backbone-amide class value borrowed from brain; primary amides (R-CONH2) typically exchange SLOWER than backbone amides (no adjacent carbonyl inductive activation of the N-H), so the true kex may be ~10-20 s-1, which would lower the already-marginal contrast. The carboxyl groups are correctly excluded (deprotonated at pH 7.4).
  • No liver-specific glutamine CEST offset was found in the literature. The chemist estimated ~3.4 ppm for the primary amide; the simulation used the generic amide class shift of 3.5 ppm. The 0.1 ppm difference is unresolved at clinical fields (4-25 Hz) and is moot given the 0 Hz overlap with protein APT anyway.
  • The amine ~2 ppm is unsimulated (no reference). The alpha-amine NH2/NH3+ (2H, ~2 ppm) is a real exchangeable group but is marked NOT SIMULATED because the reference table has no verified amine kex/shift. Its contrast cannot be claimed. No other groups neglected; carboxyls are deprotonated.

No dedicated free-glutamate liver metabolite-change study; aminotransferase/transaminase papers report enzyme activity (GOT/GPT), not free glutamate. Only an indirect Glu+Gln MRS reference available.

Caveats / critique (7 points, 310 words) — 10 mM glutamate is at the high end of the liver range (typically 2-8 mM), so the concentration may be mildly inflated, but it is not the deciding factor. The de…
  • 10 mM glutamate is at the high end of the liver range (typically 2-8 mM), so the concentration may be mildly inflated, but it is not the deciding factor. The deciding factor is chemical: glutamate's only exchangeable proton is the fast-exchanging alpha-amine, which is unsimulated. Even at 10 mM there is no sharp intermediate-exchange group to give CEST contrast.
  • CORRECT assessment. The alpha-amine NH2/NH3+ (2H, ~2 ppm) is the only exchangeable group, correctly classed 'amine' and correctly identified as fast-exchanging/broadened into water. Both carboxyls are correctly excluded (deprotonated at pH 7.4, pKa ~2.2 and ~4.3). The conclusion that glutamate is weakly/not cleanly CEST-visible in liver is sound.
  • The amine group is NOT SIMULATED (no reference), so its contrast is unknown and cannot be claimed. No exchangeable protons were neglected. No liver glutamate CEST measurement was found.
  • The GluCEST literature (PMID 30072394, 39806490) detects glutamate via the amine group in tumor/brain at ~2-3 ppm, not in liver, and the amine here is unsimulated so no in-vivo shift can be compared. The ~2 ppm chemist estimate is a solution value. None. Both carboxyls are deprotonated (correctly excluded).
  • The only exchangeable group (alpha-amine, 2H) is listed but NOT SIMULATED for lack of a reference. No additional exchangeable protons exist on glutamate. Not simulated: alpha-amine NH2/NH3+ (2H) [amine] -- the reference table has no verified exchange rate and shift for amine protons -- we don't know; not simulated
  • Chemist agent's proposed structure was WRONG and has been replaced with PubChem's verified structure for 'Glutamate'. Rejected SMILES: 'NCC(CCC(=O)O)C(=O)O'; PubChem: 'C(CC(=O)O)[C@@H](C(=O)O)N'. The exchangeable-proton groups below are still the chemist's own analysis and may have been reasoned from the wrong structure. Estimate. ~5 exchangeable protons. Needs a direct tissue-assay value to firm up.
  • [Unsourced reasoning] 1 numeric step(s) rest on an unsourced assumption: '~5 exchangeable protons (2 amine, 2 carboxyl, backbone).'.

In vivo verification: ROI-differential CEST scan — axial

Why this scan:

  • An axial slice at the renal-portal level places the liver (glycogen ~285 mM glucose-equivalent, a glycoNOE source upfield near -1 ppm; mobile amide ~50 mM at +3.5 ppm) in the same field of view as kidney, spleen and back muscle. These tissues have very different, literature-grounded concentrations of all three metabolites.
  • If a -1 ppm or +3.5 ppm offset shows ROI contrast that tracks the known concentration differences (liver >> muscle, spleen ~ liver, kidney intermediate), that is evidence the effect is real metabolite exchange, not a generic MT/NOE background that looks similar across tissues at a given offset.
ROIWhere it is drawnRole
liver target tissueROI drawn in the right hepatic lobe, away from vessels and gallbladder, on the central axial slice.Target tissue; the metabolite of interest has its highest glycogen and substantial mobile-amide content here.
renal cortexROI drawn in the outer renal cortex of the right kidney, avoiding medulla and collecting system.Comparison tissue: tabulated water/MT parameters; intermediate glycogen, moderate protein/amide and glutamine.
spleenROI drawn in the splenic parenchyma, avoiding the hilum and adjacent vessels.Comparison tissue: tabulated parameters; low glycogen, high cellular protein.
paraspinal muscleROI drawn in the right paraspinal (quadratus lumborum/multifidus) muscle at the posterior aspect, same slice.Comparison tissue: tabulated parameters; high muscle glycogen and protein, low glutamine.

Scan protocol: 3 T, pulsed Gaussian saturation train, B1=0.5 µT, 50 pulses × 50 ms (interpulse delay 100 ms, duty cycle 33.3%), total Tsat=7500 ms, TR=8000 ms

SAR reasoning (the experimentalist agent's own; the pipeline applies no SAR model): Duty-cycled 50 ms pulses at 0.5 µT with 100 ms gaps give a 33% duty cycle, well below continuous-wave SAR. Abdominal body-coil SAR at 3 T tolerates this; total Tsat of 7.5 s per offset is the main time cost, not local B1 heating.

Compromise rationale: The physicist's 3 T values were 0.25 µT/3 s (glycogen), 0.75 µT/3 s (amide), 0.75 µT/3 s (glutamine). A 0.5 µT, 7.5 s Tsat compromise favors the amide and glutamine (both want 0.75 µT) and extends saturation to 7.5 s so the 0.25 µT glycogen rNOE still reaches steady-state. It slightly under-saturates amide/glutamine versus their 0.75 µT optimum and slightly over-drives the low-B1 glycogen regime, but keeps all three in the measurable range for ROI-differential analysis.

Fat suppression: SPAIR (dual-frequency chemical shift) or SPIR prepulse. The axial upper-abdominal slice borders hepatic fat, perinephric and paraspinal fat and visceral omental fat, all of which would corrupt CEST/NOE offsets near 0-3.5 ppm and the upfield rNOE region. Water-selective excitation is added as a second guard against residual fat.

Motion mitigation: Navigator- or respiratory-triggered acquisition with a 30% window (e.g. end-expiration) to hold the diaphragmatic slice position; abdominal blooming/bowel motion also benefits. A 5-breath-hold is impractical given ~11 offsets x 7.5 s saturation plus readout, so triggered free-breathing is used, which stretches total scan time and makes the 33% duty cycle and 7.5 s Tsat the limiting factors.

Slice coverage: Axial single slice (or 3-5 mm multi-slice slab), thickness 15 mm, centred at the level of the renal hila/portal vein so it passes through the mid-liver (right lobe), both kidneys (cortex), the spleen, and the posterior paraspinal muscle in one field of view. FOV 320-360 mm.

Structures in FOV: liver, right kidney, left kidney, spleen, paraspinal muscle, aorta, vertebral body marrow, subcutaneous fat

Z-spectrum sampling offsets:

  • -8.00 ppm: far-off baseline reference
  • -5.00 ppm: far-off baseline reference
  • -3.50 ppm: Mobile protein/peptide amide pool rNOE (mobile protein aliphatic C-H relayed NOE ~-3.5 ppm), symmetric reference for amide MTRasym
  • -1.00 ppm: Glycogen rNOE / glycoCEST (~-1 ppm), symmetric reference for +1 ppm
  • -1.00 ppm: B0-correction (WASSR) reference point
  • +0.00 ppm: water (0 ppm), MTRasym denominator reference
  • +1.00 ppm: symmetric reference for -1 ppm (glycogen)
  • +2.00 ppm: Glutamine alpha-amine (broadened into water), far reference
  • +3.40 ppm: Glutamine side-chain primary amide CONH2 (~3.4 ppm), symmetric reference for -3.4 ppm
  • +3.50 ppm: Mobile protein/peptide amide APT backbone NH (~3.5 ppm), symmetric reference for -3.5 ppm
  • +5.00 ppm: far-off baseline reference
  • +8.00 ppm: far-off baseline reference

Differential analysis plan:

  • For each ROI, build a B0-corrected Z-spectrum (WASSR reference at the -1 ppm point) and compute MTRasym = (S(-offset)-S(+offset))/S(0) at +3.5, +3.4, +1.0 and -3.5/-1.0. Compare the MTRasym/Lorentzian-difference amplitude at each metabolite offset across the four ROIs.
  • Confirming signature: at +3.5/+3.4 ppm and -3.5 ppm the amide-related amplitude should be roughly similar across ROIs (mobile protein is present in all) but slightly modulated by the known 40-60 mM differences at -1 ppm the amplitude should track the known glycogen gradient (liver highest, then spleen, muscle, kidney) with the liver clearly above the others
  • at the glutamine offsets, amplitude should track 7/5/3/15 mM (muscle highest, spleen lowest). A pattern where the same offset's ROI contrast scales with the independently known concentration difference, while a far-off offset (+/-8 ppm) shows no such scaling, is evidence of metabolite-specific exchange.
  • Inconclusive if all ROIs show similar contrast at every offset (background MT/NOE) or if the -1 ppm liver-muscle gap is lost to partial volume.

Not actively targeted: ATP, inorganic phosphate and glutamate were not actively designed around: the physicist reported low/no simulated CEST contrast for them at any field strength and they fall outside this scan's budget. Glutamate's amide/amine shifts largely overlap the glutamine and mobile-amide regions already sampled here, so any glutamate contribution is subsumed in the +3.4/+3.5 ppm analysis rather than given a dedicated offset.

Caveats:

  • Partial volume is the main threat: the paraspinal-muscle ROI is thin and borders fat and bone, and the liver ROI can pick up vessel/gallbladder, so the -1 ppm glycogen differential (liver only ~modestly above muscle) is the weakest. B0/B1 inhomogeneity across ROIs persists even after WASSR correction, and the 0.7x-1.3x B1 re-simulation will show how much survives transmit-field variation.
  • Susceptibility from the posterior vertebrae and from bowel gas can distort the upfield (-1 to -3.5 ppm) region. Finally, one compromise B1 (0.5 µT) and Tsat (7.5 s) cannot be simultaneously optimal for the 0.25 µT glycogen regime and the 0.75 µT amide/glutamine regime, so contrast for each metabolite is a trade-off, not a maximum.
